narrativeReportMd:
# time R4→R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
A local hard instance-breaking change was found for `time.value`: R6 limits fractional seconds to 1-9 digits, while R4 allowed one or more digits with no explicit upper bound. R4 data containing more than 9 fractional-second digits can be valid under the R4 regex but invalid under the R6 regex.

## Scope
I compared the R4 and R6 core package StructureDefinitions for `http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/time`, their package/index metadata, and the R6 `PrimitiveType` base artifact only to classify the inheritance shift. Inherited/base-artifact changes are excluded from local findings as instructed.

## Main migration themes
The primitive's identity and instance shape are otherwise stable: the same `time`, `time.id`, `time.extension`, and `time.value` elements remain with the same local cardinalities, types, modifier flags, summary flags, and XML-attribute representation. Migration work is concentrated on detecting or normalizing over-precision fractional seconds.

## Highest-impact findings
- `time:value-constraint:time.value:fractional-precision-9`: R6 changes the regex from `([01][0-9]|2[0-3]):[0-5][0-9]:([0-5][0-9]|60)(\.[0-9]+)?` to `([01][0-9]|2[0-3]):[0-5][0-9]:([0-5][0-9]|60)(\.[0-9]{1,9})?`.

## Findings requiring human review
No finding requires human review to identify the model change. Implementers with existing over-precision data still need a local policy for rejecting, rounding, or truncating those values.

## Backward-compatible design observations
The precision cap is plausibly intended to make the primitive bounded and interoperable, but the supplied inputs do not include an official rationale. A less disruptive path could have introduced warnings or implementation guidance before making the regex narrower.

## Follow-up analysis
Assess the R6 `PrimitiveType`/`DataType` hierarchy change in the corresponding base-artifact report so code generation and inheritance risks are deduplicated across primitive datatype reports.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: R6 preserves the `time` primitive identity and shape but narrows the local value regex, creating a hard R4→R6 validation break for times with more than 9 fractional-second digits. The main migration concern is precision policy for rare over-precision values; the main uncertainty is the absence of an official change rationale.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Existing R4 systems should scan `time` values for fractional seconds longer than 9 digits before R6 validation. Values with 0-9 fractional digits, leap-second seconds value `60`, and no timezone remain aligned with the computable regex. Any truncation or rounding should be explicit and tested because it changes the literal primitive value.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for the structural and validation comparison because both assigned StructureDefinitions are present and the material change is directly visible in the `time.value` regex extension in both snapshot and differential. Confidence about why HL7 made the change is lower because no official diff, ballot reconciliation note, or narrative page was supplied.

findings.title: R6 limits time fractional seconds to at most 9 digits

oldState.summary: R4 `time.value` used a regex with an unbounded fractional-second digit count.
oldState.narrativeMd: In R4, a `time` value could include a fractional second with one or more digits after the decimal point. The regex did not declare an upper precision limit.

newState.summary: R6 `time.value` uses a regex capped at 1-9 fractional-second digits.
newState.narrativeMd: In R6, the fractional part remains optional, but if present it must contain between 1 and 9 digits.

facts.oldValue: 1..unbounded when a fractional part is present
facts.newValue: 1..9 when a fractional part is present

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The old and new elements have the same ElementDefinition id and path, `time.value`, with the same primitive FHIRPath type. The only local value-domain difference is the regex quantifier on the fractional-second digits.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct validation break for the subset of R4 instances whose `time` literals contain more than 9 fractional-second digits. Such a value matches the R4 regex but fails the R6 regex. Runtime risk is medium because strict validators, generated primitive wrappers, database constraints, or parsing libraries updated from R4 to R6 may newly reject values they previously accepted; prevalence is likely low but data-dependent.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The main risk is data loss or rejection if a migration silently truncates or rounds sub-nanosecond precision. For most clinical and administrative `time` values this is unlikely to be safety-critical, but systems that preserve device or measurement timestamps should apply an explicit precision policy.

justification.inferredGoal: Bound the primitive's fractional-second precision, likely to improve interoperability and implementation consistency.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the R4 regex temporarily and add a base warning or advisory 9-digit precision limit.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal is reasonable: capping fractional-second precision at 9 digits gives validators, parsers, generated types, databases, and comparison logic a bounded lexical space. The break affects only R4 values with more than 9 fractional-second digits, which are likely uncommon, but it is still a real R4-to-R6 validation break. A less-breaking path exists only if R6 accepted a weaker transition design. Because that alternative would leave arbitrary precision valid in the base datatype and therefore fail to guarantee the consistency the change appears to seek, the break is probably justified despite the absence of an official rationale in the supplied inputs.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base R6 design would be to retain the R4 `time.value` regex for one release while adding a warning-level invariant, advisory rule, or clear normative guidance that precision beyond 9 fractional-second digits is discouraged and may become invalid later. That would preserve all R4-valid literals during transition. Ordinary migration transforms, profile-only restrictions, or extensions preserving the original literal are mitigations rather than backward-compatible base-design alternatives, so they do not make this a `Yes`. The material tradeoff is that base R6 implementations would still need to accept and store arbitrary-length fractional seconds, and systems could not rely on a uniform base precision cap.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This preserves over-precision R4 literals, but base R6 would still lack an enforceable bounded precision rule.

evidence.detail: R4 regex allows one or more fractional-second digits with `[0-9]+`.
R6 regex allows only 1 through 9 fractional-second digits with `[0-9]{1,9}`.
The same R4 regex appears in the differential, confirming it is local to `time.value` rather than only inherited snapshot content.
The same R6 regex appears in the differential, confirming the precision cap is a local `time.value` definition.

examples.examplesMd: `12:34:56.1234567890` is an illustrative primitive value: it has 10 fractional-second digits, so it matches R4's unbounded fractional-second regex and fails R6's 1-9 digit regex. The migration example shows truncation only as one possible policy; systems should not silently truncate without confirming that loss of precision is acceptable.

findings.narrativeMd: `time.value` became narrower in R6 because the fractional-second part is now capped at 9 digits. Implementers who stored or accepted arbitrary precision in R4 can encounter new validation failures even though the element name, cardinality, primitive type, and representation did not change. This can be surprising because common values such as `12:34:56` and `12:34:56.123` still work, while only over-precision values fail.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-valid primitive value such as `12:34:56.1234567890` can become R6-invalid. The reverse direction is not materially affected by this local change: every R6 value that satisfies the 1-9 digit fractional limit also satisfies the R4 regex. Strict parsers, generated primitive classes, JSON schema-like validators, database CHECK constraints, or FHIRPath literal handling that enforce the regex are the likely mechanisms where the break appears.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Before R6 validation, scan all elements typed as `time` for a decimal fraction longer than 9 digits. Decide whether to reject those records, round them, truncate them, or preserve the original literal in an extension or audit trail. A transform from more than 9 digits to 9 digits is not lossless, so test boundary cases with no fraction, 1 digit, 9 digits, 10 digits, and leap-second values such as `23:59:60.1234567890`.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The same interoperability goal could have been pursued less disruptively by keeping the R4 regex and adding a warning invariant, implementation guidance, or an R6 profile that limits precision. That alternative would keep all R4-valid literals accepted by the base datatype, but it would not give base R6 implementations a single bounded precision rule.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The finding is based on the computable regex extension. An official narrative page or ballot change note could confirm whether the intended precision limit is specifically nanoseconds or another implementation-driven cap.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 narrows the lexical value space for `time.value`: an R4 time such as `12:34:56.1234567890` has a valid fractional second under the R4 regex but is invalid under the R6 regex because R6 caps the fraction at 9 digits. That is a real old-valid/new-invalid break for strict validators and primitive parsers. The affected slice is narrow, though: ordinary second, millisecond, microsecond, and nanosecond times remain valid, and the same 9-digit cap appears to be part of a broader R6 temporal-primitive consistency change. Because the likely interoperability goal is an enforceable bounded precision and the break only affects sub-nanosecond or arbitrary-precision literals, the change is breaking but appears proportionate.
keyEvidence: R4 `StructureDefinition-time.json` `time.value` regex is `([01][0-9]|2[0-3]):[0-5][0-9]:([0-5][0-9]|60)(\.[0-9]+)?`, allowing any positive number of fractional-second digits.
R6 `StructureDefinition-time.json` `time.value` regex is `([01][0-9]|2[0-3]):[0-5][0-9]:([0-5][0-9]|60)(\.[0-9]{1,9})?`, allowing only 1 through 9 fractional-second digits.
The regex difference is present in both snapshot and differential for `time.value`, so this is a local value constraint change rather than inherited noise.
R4 and R6 `StructureDefinition-time.json` both carry `structuredefinition-standards-status` = `normative` and `structuredefinition-normative-version` = `4.0.0`.
Local comparison of R6 `time`, `dateTime`, and `instant` definitions shows the same `{1,9}` fractional-second cap across temporal primitive regexes.
freshReview.fmmEffect: The supplied R4 maturity context and the StructureDefinition metadata indicate normative content, so the hard validation break carries a high stability burden. That pushed the review away from dismissing the change as minor, but the break applies only to values with more than 9 fractional-second digits and appears tied to a consistent primitive precision rule, so normative status alone did not make it a Revisit.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 instances containing `time` values with more than 9 fractional-second digits can newly fail R6 validation or parsing. Reverse R6-to-R4 representability is not a concern for this specific constraint because the R6 value space is a subset of the R4 regex.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking base design could have retained the R4 unbounded regex for one release and added warning-level guidance discouraging precision beyond 9 digits. That would preserve all R4-valid literals, but it would not deliver an enforceable base R6 precision cap and would keep arbitrary-length fractional seconds in validators, parsers, storage constraints, and comparison code. Profile-only rules, migration transforms, or preserving the original literal in an extension are mitigations rather than less-breaking base R6 designs. Overall, the alternative is plausible but has material tradeoffs and is not clearly preferable.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree: the existing report correctly identifies a hard R4-to-R6 instance break, likely rare prevalence, and only a partial less-breaking alternative. The fresh review reaches the same practical conclusion while giving normative status explicit weight.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, abstract flag, active status, derivation, normative status, and normative version are stable. The baseDefinition changed from `Element` to `PrimitiveType`, but that is treated as an out-of-scope base/infrastructure issue.
Both snapshots contain the same local element paths: `time`, `time.id`, `time.extension`, and `time.value`; no local element was added, removed, renamed, moved, split, or merged.
`time.value` remains `http://hl7.org/fhirpath/System.Time` with FHIR type `time`; `time.id` remains FHIRPath `System.String`; `time.extension` remains `Extension`.
`time` has no Reference-typed elements or target profiles.
`time` has no terminology bindings, so there is no binding strength or value set change to assess.

No local invariant was added or removed for `time.value`. Inherited `ele-1` human text and R4 `xpath` metadata differ in the snapshots, but those are inherited `Element`/base-definition concerns and are out of local scope.
No fixed value, pattern value, or default value appears on the local `time` elements in either version.
`isModifier` remains `false` for the root, `id`, `extension`, and `value` elements.
`isSummary` remains `false` where present for the `time` elements.
The local `time` StructureDefinition does not introduce slicing changes. Any slicing shown on the R6 `PrimitiveType.extension` base artifact is out of local `time` scope.

The core definition remains `A time during the day, with no date specified`. The R6 StructureDefinition description drops the R4 prefix `Base StructureDefinition for`, which is not a semantic constraint change.

`time.value` remains represented as an XML attribute in the StructureDefinition. No local JSON/XML element-name or primitive wrapper representation change was found; the material change is validation of the literal value, not serialization shape.
For the local regex change, the R6 lexical space is a subset of the R4 lexical space. R6-valid `time` literals with 0-9 fractional digits are representable as R4 `time` literals.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds type-characteristics metadata to time
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R6 adds StructureDefinition metadata extensions declaring `time` to have range, continuous, and length characteristics. These are not instance elements, cardinality constraints, or lexical restrictions, so they do not by themselves make R4 instances invalid.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Tooling that consumes StructureDefinition metadata may expose additional comparison, range, or length behavior for `time`. Treat this as metadata awareness rather than an instance transform requirement.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 updates publication metadata without changing the primitive identity
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The publisher/contact/jurisdiction/experimental metadata changed in the R6 ballot package, but the canonical URL, type, kind, status, and normative status remain stable. These metadata changes do not affect instance validation for `time`.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Consumers that display package metadata may show `HL7 International / FHIR Infrastructure`, world jurisdiction, and `experimental: false` for the R6 ballot definition.

Inherited `Element` constraint text and inherited `id`/`extension` details appear in the `time` snapshots but are not local to `time`; they should be covered by the base `Element` analysis if material.
